deep.reconstruction:
The page is headed 'Causalität'. It contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a philosophical fragment in three parts.

(A) Four numbered theses on what an agent (Agens) can be.
- I. What an agent strives to bring about must be determined by the concept of the agent alone. Its action can depend only on its own essence.
- II. This requirement is met if the agent strives to preserve or restore itself (sich selbst zu erhalten oder herzustellen).
- III. Such self-preserving action is conceivable only if the agent is a state (Zustand) or a relation (Verhältniss), not a thing or substance (Ding, Stoff). The argument: striving to preserve or restore X presupposes that deviations from X, in varying degrees, are possible. Where this striving conflicts with other strivings, X is only maintained or restored 'as nearly as possible'. Substance admits no degrees; only states or relations admit gradual difference. So a self-preserving agent must be a state or relation.
- IV. Such action can only operate on things capable of the same kind of state or relation. Whether it acts at all, and on which of those things, cannot be inferred from the concept of the agent.

Implicit physical reading (mine, interpretive): the agent behaves like a restoring tendency toward an equilibrium state. Competing tendencies give a compromise, a 'nearest possible' state, i.e. a minimum or extremum of some measure of deviation. This matches Riemann's ether-based natural philosophy, where forces arise from the medium's tendency to restore a state. It also anticipates the reference to the principle of least action below. The self-preservation motif is recognisably Herbart's (Selbsterhaltung der Realen), adapted. Riemann insists the bearer of self-preservation is a state or relation rather than a simple real.

(B) Critique of Kant.
- Riemann agrees with Kant that analysing the concept of a thing cannot reveal that it exists or that it causes another thing. Being and causality are therefore not analytic and must come from experience.
- He rejects Kant's later move: deriving the causal concept from an a priori constitution of the knowing subject, and reducing it to a mere rule of temporal succession. Under that rule any perception could be linked as cause with any other as effect. Riemann says this 'throws out the baby with the bathwater'.
- His own view: causal relations must be taken from experience, but reflection should correct and complete our grasp of these empirical facts.

(C) Terminological note on 'actio'.
- German renders both actio and effectus as 'Wirkung'. Because the 'effect' sense dominates, ambiguity arises, e.g. in translating 'actio aequalis est reactioni' (Newton's third law) and 'principium actionis minimae' (least action, Maupertuis/Euler/Lagrange).
- Kant adds the Latin 'actio', 'actio mutua' in brackets after 'Wirkung' and 'Wechselwirkung'.
- Riemann considers 'Kraft ist gleich der Gegenkraft' and 'Satz vom kleinsten Kraftaufwande'. Since German lacks a simple word for agere, he asks leave to use the foreign word.
- A later note in different ink adds that in his earlier writings Kant translates actio as 'Handlung'.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible: the page contains no computations.
Philosophically, thesis III's step from 'no degrees of substance' to 'the agent must be a state or relation' is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Rendering 'principium actionis minimae' as 'Satz vom kleinsten Kraftaufwande' is loose: the Maupertuis-Euler-Lagrange action is not an expenditure of force. Riemann offers it only tentatively ('man könnte vielleicht sagen') and then rejects such renderings in favour of the Latin word.

results.what: Theses that a causal agent must be a self-preserving or self-restoring state or relation, admitting degrees of deviation and restored 'as nearly as possible' under competing tendencies.
results.modern_name: Philosophy of causation; restoring-tendency or equilibrium conception of force (cf. Herbart's Selbsterhaltung)
results.usually_credited_to: Herbart (Selbsterhaltung of the reals, 1820s); Riemann's Herbartian natural philosophy

results.what: Critique of Kant's a priori, time-succession account of causality ('das Kind mit dem Bade ausschütten'). Causal relations come from experience but are refined by reflection.
results.modern_name: Empiricist-critical response to Kant's Second Analogy

results.what: Terminological remark on translating actio (Newton's third law, principle of least action) as 'Wirkung', and Kant's practice.
results.modern_name: History of terminology: action/reaction, least action

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a purely philosophical fragment consistent with Riemann's known Herbartian natural-philosophy fragments, parts of which Weber/Dedekind printed in the Gesammelte Werke; whether this particular passage was printed is unsure. It contains no mathematics. Its interest is biographical: it shows explicit anti-Kantian views on causality and a self-preservation conception of agents, both already known in outline.
transcription_corrections: 'Fände ein Streben' is probably 'Findet ein Streben' (or 'Bestreben'); the word is underlined in the image.
'zu einer bloßen Regel der Zeitfolge herabsetzt[?]': the verb in the image looks more like 'stempelt' ('zu einer bloßen Regel der Zeitfolge stempelt').
The interlinear insertion in the Kant sentence is uncertain. It may read 'Sein und Causalitätsverhältniss nicht Merkmale seien'; trust the image.
The final marginal addition probably reads 'wie es auch Anderen gestattet worden' rather than 'wie auch etwas Anderes gestattet werden'.
The last line ('In seinen früheren Schriften übersetzt er actio durch Handlung') is in a different, brownish ink and was evidently added later.
In thesis III an insertion appears above 'Zustand oder ein Verhältniss' (possibly 'wirklicher' or similar); it is omitted in the machine transcription.
